title: Acceleration due to gravity with a simple pendulum
settings: Bob treated as a point mass; string mass and stretching neglected.
Fixed amplitude: 3° for the example report.
Time is for 20 complete cycles and rounded to 0.01 s.
modelExtra: The timing model includes the leading finite-amplitude correction T ≈ 2π√(L/g)[1 + θ₀²/16 + 11θ₀⁴/3072], with θ₀ in radians. The simple graph analysis neglects this correction, giving a small systematic bias even at 3°. Angles above 5° remain available for exploration but cannot be recorded.
aim: Determine gravitational acceleration from the gradient of a graph of period squared against pendulum length.
intro: Turn the familiar motion of a swinging bob into a quantitative measurement. You will vary length, time 20 complete oscillations at each setting, calculate period, and use a straight-line graph to estimate g. The displayed timing run is accelerated virtual time; its readings are generated by an ideal model, not observations of a physical pendulum.

apparatus.name: Bob and light string
apparatus.purpose: Concentrate the moving mass in a small bob suspended from a string whose mass and extension can be neglected.

apparatus.name: Rigid support and clamp
apparatus.purpose: Provide a fixed pivot and allow the effective pendulum length to be changed.

apparatus.name: Metre rule and angle guide
apparatus.purpose: Measure pivot-to-bob-centre length in metres and set an initial angle no larger than 5 degrees.

apparatus.name: Timer and reference marker
apparatus.purpose: Measure elapsed time for 20 complete oscillations using a consistent crossing and direction.

topics.title: What counts as one oscillation?
topics.text: A period is the time to return to the same position with the same direction of motion. Starting at the centre moving right, the next centre crossing moving left is only half a period. Count full cycles by watching one centre crossing direction. Frequency is the number of full cycles per second; angular frequency measures phase change in radians per second.
topics.question: Is a left-to-right centre crossing followed by a right-to-left crossing one complete oscillation?
topics.answer: No. It is half an oscillation. Wait for the next left-to-right crossing to complete the cycle.

topics.title: Restoring force and the small-angle model
topics.text: The component of gravity along the bob's arc pulls it toward equilibrium. Tension acts along the string, keeping the motion on the arc. Dividing tangential acceleration by length gives theta-double-dot = -(g/L)sin(theta). For small angles in radians, replace sin(theta) by theta; this creates the linear equation of simple harmonic motion. Use an initial angle at most 5 degrees so this approximation is appropriate. The simulation uses this limiting equation rather than modelling the small finite-amplitude correction.
topics.question: Why keep the release angle small?
topics.answer: The linear period formula relies on sin(theta) approximately equalling theta; large swings have a longer period than this model predicts.

topics.title: Effective length and mass independence
topics.text: The effective length L runs from the pivot to the bob's centre of mass, not just along the exposed string. In the point-bob model the same bob mass appears in the gravitational force and inertia, so it cancels. Increasing bob mass alone therefore does not change the model period. A large bob, a heavy string, or a flexible support changes the physical system and may require a more complete description.
topics.question: Should you measure to the top or centre of the bob?
topics.answer: Measure from the pivot to the centre of mass, approximately the geometric centre for a uniform spherical bob.
topics.formula: L = pivot-to-centre distance; T is independent of bob mass

topics.title: Why time 20 cycles?
topics.text: A single stopwatch start-and-stop interval has endpoint reaction error. Spreading that interval over N = 20 cycles reduces its contribution to the period uncertainty by the factor N. It does not remove a miscount, a biased timer, or a length error. Record repeated 20-cycle runs at each length, average their elapsed times, then divide by 20. The virtual timer is a teaching tool and has no human reaction time unless an explicit noise model is added.
topics.question: Does a timer with a 0.01 s display guarantee a 0.01 s physical timing uncertainty?
topics.answer: No. Resolution is only one contribution; reaction time, cycle counting and run-to-run scatter can dominate.

topics.title: Straight-line analysis
topics.text: Squaring the period formula gives T squared proportional to L. Plot L in metres on the horizontal axis and T squared in seconds squared on the vertical axis. Fit y = mL + b using several well-spaced lengths. The gradient has units s squared per metre, and g is 4pi squared divided by the gradient. The ideal intercept is zero. Fit an intercept initially: a persistent nonzero value can flag a fixed length offset or another systematic effect, although a zero intercept alone does not prove accuracy.
topics.question: What is the unit of the graph gradient?
topics.answer: Seconds squared per metre, because the vertical quantity is T squared and the horizontal quantity is length.

topics.title: Uncertainty and responsible conclusions
topics.text: For a timing-derived period, the first-order uncertainty in T squared is 2T u(T). If the fitted gradient has uncertainty u(m), the relative gradient contribution to u(g) equals u(m)/m. Length uncertainty also matters: an ordinary least-squares fit treats horizontal coordinates as exact, so use a suitable fit or discuss that limitation when length errors are significant. The model uses g = 9.80665 m/s squared as a reference parameter, not a measured local value. Perfect virtual agreement tests the algebra and software; it does not establish laboratory accuracy.
topics.question: Can perfectly collinear simulated points justify reporting zero uncertainty for a real experiment?
topics.answer: No. They show consistency of the ideal generator; a physical experiment still has timing, length, alignment and model uncertainties.
topics.formula: u(T^2) approximately 2T u(T); u(g)/g approximately u(m)/m (gradient contribution)

procedure.title: Define the length
procedure.text: Set a pivot-to-bob-centre length and record L in metres. Begin near the middle of the available range.
procedure.why: Using the string length alone produces a systematic length error.

procedure.title: Set a small release
procedure.text: Displace the bob by no more than 5 degrees. Release it without a push and keep motion in a single vertical plane.
procedure.why: A small, clean release matches the assumed simple harmonic motion.

procedure.title: Time 20 cycles
procedure.text: Choose one direction of crossing at the centre. Start at crossing zero and finish at crossing 20 in the same direction. Read the elapsed virtual time in seconds.
procedure.why: A consistent phase and cycle count avoids half-period and off-by-one errors.

procedure.title: Repeat and vary length
procedure.text: Repeat timings if available, then use at least five lengths across the permitted range. Keep the angle small for every run.
procedure.why: Repeats assess scatter and a spread of lengths constrains the graph gradient.

procedure.title: Process observations
procedure.text: For each length calculate mean elapsed time, T = mean time/20, and T squared. Keep unrounded values for the fit and round only table display values.
procedure.why: Early rounding can bias the gradient and the final estimate.

procedure.title: Fit and interpret
procedure.text: Fit T squared against L with an intercept. Calculate g = 4pi squared/gradient, state units, inspect the intercept and residuals, and discuss uncertainties before comparing with the model reference.
procedure.why: A reported result needs both a numerical estimate and an assessment of what the data support.

precautions: Measure length to the bob centre at eye level to reduce parallax.
Use a rigid support and a light, taut string; avoid rubbing at the pivot.
Release without a push, use at most 5 degrees, and avoid elliptical motion.
Count full cycles in the same direction and record virtual readings as simulated data.

quiz.question: If length is multiplied by four, what happens to the ideal period?
quiz.explanation: The period is proportional to the square root of length.

quiz.question: Which graph gives g directly from a straight-line gradient m through g = 4pi squared/m?
quiz.explanation: Squaring T = 2pi sqrt(L/g) makes the gradient 4pi squared/g.

quiz.question: What is the correct effective pendulum length?
options: Pivot to centre of mass of bob
quiz.explanation: The point-mass model places the bob mass at its centre of mass.

limitations: This virtual experiment assumes a point bob, a massless inextensible string, a fixed frictionless pivot, planar small-angle motion and uniform gravity. It neglects damping, finite-bob inertia, support movement and finite-amplitude period changes. Timing displays represent accelerated simulated time rather than wall-clock measurements. Rounded model readings may create small fit residuals; these are not empirical measurement uncertainty. The reference 9.80665 m/s squared is a chosen standard model parameter, not a claim about gravity at your location.

title: Moment of inertia by bifilar suspension
settings: Uniform slender rod: mass M = 0.500 kg; rod length ℓ = 0.500 m.
Half-separation a = 0.100 m; full separation d = 2a = 0.200 m.
Reference gravity g = 9.80665 m s⁻²; example yaw amplitude 3°.
modelExtra: Equal, parallel strings are attached symmetrically about the centre of mass. The model uses the small-yaw relation T = 2π√[IL/(Mga²)]. It assumes negligible string mass, rod width, damping and support compliance. The simulated target inertia is Mℓ²/12. Angles above 5° cannot be recorded.
aim: Determine the moment of inertia of a uniform slender rod about its vertical centre-of-mass axis from bifilar oscillations at different string lengths.
intro: Suspend a horizontal rod from two equal parallel strings and twist it gently about the vertical axis through its centre. Use changes in period with string length to infer rotational inertia. The virtual rod has mass 0.500 kg, length 0.500 m, and suspension points 0.200 m apart. The animation is accelerated and the timing observations are generated, not physical measurements.

apparatus.name: Uniform slender rod
apparatus.purpose: Supply the rotating test body: mass M = 0.500 kg and rod length D = 0.500 m.

apparatus.name: Two strings and rigid overhead support
apparatus.purpose: Suspend the rod horizontally using equal strings and matching top and bottom separation 2a = 0.200 m.

apparatus.name: Rule and balance
apparatus.purpose: Measure equilibrium string length L, half-separation a, rod length D, and rod mass M.

apparatus.name: Timer and angular marker
apparatus.purpose: Time 20 small torsional cycles using a consistent orientation and direction.

topics.title: Inertia depends on the chosen axis
topics.text: Rotational inertia weights each small mass element by the square of its perpendicular distance from an axis. This experiment uses the vertical axis through the rod centre, perpendicular to its length. For a uniform slender rod of length D, integration gives I = MD squared/12. With M = 0.500 kg and D = 0.500 m, the model value is 0.0104167 kg m squared. A finite-width rectangular bar instead has I = M(D squared + w squared)/12; ignoring width is justified only for a slender rod.
topics.question: Would the same rod have the same inertia about one end?
topics.answer: No. Moving the parallel axis to an end adds M(D/2) squared by the parallel-axis theorem.

topics.title: Bifilar geometry and the factor of four
topics.text: Here a is half the string separation, so the two strings are 2a = 0.200 m apart. Both upper attachments must be directly above their corresponding lower attachments at equilibrium. L is their common equilibrium length, not the rod length D. Using full separation in a formula written for half-separation gives an inertia four times too large.
topics.question: If the strings are 0.200 m apart, what a belongs in our equation?
topics.answer: a = 0.100 m. The symbol denotes half the separation.
topics.formula: d = 2a; a = 0.100 m; L = equilibrium string length

topics.title: Why a twisted rod returns
topics.text: A gentle twist moves the lower attachment points sideways and lifts the rod slightly. Its increased gravitational potential energy supplies the restoring tendency. For small theta, the lift is approximately a squared theta squared/(2L). Differentiating Mg times this lift gives a restoring torque -(Mga squared/L)theta. Thin flexible strings are assumed to supply negligible material torsional stiffness.
topics.question: Is gravity absent because the rod rotates approximately horizontally?
topics.answer: No. The small rise during a twist changes gravitational potential energy and creates the restoring torque.
topics.formula: delta z approximately a^2 theta^2/(2L); torque approximately -(Mga^2/L)theta

topics.title: Period of the rotational oscillation
topics.text: Combining the restoring torque with I times angular acceleration gives a simple harmonic oscillator. A larger inertia slows the oscillation, longer strings weaken the restoring torque, and greater attachment separation strengthens it. Keep twists small and avoid sideways swinging or tilting so that one rotational mode dominates. A timing interval must include 20 full returns to the same orientation and direction.
topics.question: What happens to period if L doubles while all other quantities remain fixed?
topics.answer: It increases by a factor of the square root of two.

topics.title: Recover inertia from a graph
topics.text: Plot period squared vertically against string length horizontally. If T squared = mL + b, the gradient is 4pi squared I/(Mga squared). Thus I = mMga squared/(4pi squared); the gradient unit is seconds squared per metre and the resulting inertia unit is kg m squared. The ideal intercept is zero. Do not force it to zero before examining possible length offsets or effects omitted by the model.
topics.question: Does the graph horizontal axis contain rod length or string length?
topics.answer: String length L. Rod length D stays fixed and is used only in the independent theoretical inertia calculation.

topics.title: Uncertainty, comparison and evidence
topics.text: Because I depends on a squared, a small fractional separation error contributes twice that fractional error to I. For independent inputs, combine relative standard uncertainties from gradient, mass, g and twice the half-separation uncertainty in quadrature. A physical comparison with MD squared/12 must also include rod dimension and mass uncertainty. Perfect virtual agreement is expected because the data generator uses that rod formula; it is a consistency exercise rather than independent experimental confirmation.
topics.question: Why measure string separation carefully?
topics.answer: The inferred inertia is proportional to its square, so a fractional separation error is doubled to first order.

procedure.title: Record rod properties
procedure.text: Record M = 0.500 kg, D = 0.500 m and theoretical I = MD squared/12. Identify the vertical axis through the centre.
procedure.why: The theoretical comparison must refer to the same axis as the motion.

procedure.title: Align the suspension
procedure.text: Set equal string lengths L. Keep the rod horizontal, with upper and lower attachment separations both 0.200 m and centred about the rod midpoint.
procedure.why: This establishes equal parallel strings with a = 0.100 m, matching the formula.

procedure.title: Excite one small mode
procedure.text: Twist the rod only a few degrees about its central vertical axis and release without a push. Avoid lateral swinging and rocking.
procedure.why: The small-angle theory assumes predominantly torsional motion.

procedure.title: Time 20 full oscillations
procedure.text: Start at a chosen orientation moving in one direction and stop after 20 returns in the same direction. Record the generated time; repeat if available.
procedure.why: Using a fixed phase prevents half-cycle counting and spreads endpoint timing uncertainty over many cycles.

procedure.title: Vary string length
procedure.text: Use at least five well-spaced values of L while retaining the same rod and attachment spacing. Recheck equal lengths and horizontality each time; calculate T = mean time/20 and T squared.
procedure.why: Only L should vary when measuring the T squared versus L relationship.

procedure.title: Fit and compare
procedure.text: Fit T squared = mL + b. Calculate I = mMga squared/(4pi squared), inspect intercept and residuals, and compare with 0.0104167 kg m squared with suitable uncertainty discussion.
procedure.why: The gradient supplies the measured-model estimate; a comparison needs assumptions and uncertainty to be meaningful.

precautions: Keep equal string lengths and matching symmetric upper and lower attachment separations.
Use half-separation a = 0.100 m, not the full 0.200 m separation, in the stated formula.
Use small twists and reject runs showing lateral swing, rocking, slipping attachments or slack strings.
Keep clamps secure and distinguish accelerated generated timing from measurements on a real apparatus.

quiz.question: The two strings are 20 cm apart. What value of a belongs in this lesson's formula?
quiz.explanation: The formula uses half the separation: a = 0.20/2 = 0.10 m.

quiz.question: Which axis is used for the rod inertia MD squared/12?
options: Vertical through its centre, perpendicular to its length
quiz.explanation: The centred bifilar twist rotates about the central vertical axis.

quiz.question: What should vary to make the required straight-line graph?
options: String length L while rod and spacing stay fixed
quiz.explanation: T squared is proportional to L when I, M, g and a are fixed.

limitations: The model assumes a rigid uniform slender rod, equal massless inextensible strings, symmetric attachment points, matching upper and lower separation, a horizontal equilibrium rod and small isolated torsional motion. It ignores string torsional stiffness, damping, attachment inertia, finite rod width, mode coupling and support movement. The reference g is 9.80665 m/s squared. Generated readings and accelerated animation cannot reproduce the alignment difficulties or measurement uncertainty of a physical suspension. A finite-width bar requires the appropriate inertia formula; the half-separation convention must be checked before comparing with any other apparatus.

title: Young’s modulus of a wire
settings: Initial measured wire length L₀ = 2.000 m.
Circular wire diameter d = 0.500 mm; area A = πd²/4.
Extension increments are rounded to 0.001 mm; force values are exact in this model.
modelExtra: The unknown model modulus is 200 GPa. A light initial preload defines the reference length; F and δ are additional increments relative to that reference. All loads stay in the linear elastic regime. The diagram exaggerates extension. Creep, temperature drift, backlash and plastic deformation are omitted.
aim: Determine the Young modulus of a wire from its extension under a series of increasing tensile forces, and interpret the gradient of an extension–force graph.
intro: A metal wire may look rigid while extending by a fraction of a millimetre. This experiment makes that small deformation measurable. Measure the wire geometry, increase the force in steps, record extension relative to a reference, and use the complete set of readings to estimate stiffness of the material. The virtual specimen is 2.000 m long and 0.500 mm in diameter; its model Young modulus is 200 GPa.

apparatus.name: Wire and rigid support
apparatus.purpose: Provide a straight specimen with a defined 2.000 m gauge length and a secure upper clamp.

apparatus.name: Load system or calibrated force gauge
apparatus.purpose: Apply additional tensile force from 2 to 20 N in controlled increments.

apparatus.name: Micrometer screw gauge
apparatus.purpose: Measure the small diameter at several positions and orientations before calculating cross-sectional area.

apparatus.name: Extension indicator and length scale
apparatus.purpose: Record the initial gauge length and changes in length relative to a fixed reference.

topics.title: Force and stress: why wire thickness matters
topics.text: The same hanging force acts through every section of an ideal straight wire in static equilibrium when its own weight is neglected. Dividing this force by the original cross-sectional area gives tensile stress. A thin wire therefore experiences greater stress than a thick wire under the same force. Stress tells us how intensely the material is loaded, rather than describing the load alone. Use force in newtons and area in square metres to obtain pascals.
topics.question: If the diameter doubles while force stays fixed, what happens to stress?
topics.answer: The area becomes four times as large, so the stress becomes one quarter as large.

topics.title: Extension and strain: why original length matters
topics.text: Extension is the increase in gauge length, measured from a chosen reference. Strain divides that increase by the original gauge length, so two specimens of different lengths can be compared fairly. An extension of 0.50 mm is a much smaller fractional change for a two-metre wire than for a short wire. Convert both lengths to matching units before taking their ratio. Strain has no unit.
topics.question: What is the strain for 0.50 mm extension of a 2.000 m wire?
topics.answer: Convert 0.50 mm to 0.00050 m, then divide by 2.000 m: the strain is 0.00025.

topics.title: Young modulus and the linear range
topics.text: Young modulus relates tensile stress to strain within the straight portion of the material response. Larger modulus means smaller strain for a given stress. This model keeps every selected load within a linear elastic range, so removing the added load restores the reference length. In a physical specimen, elastic recovery and strict proportionality must be checked; an elastic response need not remain perfectly linear at every stress.
topics.question: Does changing the wire length change the material's Young modulus?
topics.answer: No. It changes the wire's extension for a given force, while modulus describes the material under the stated conditions.

topics.title: From a material law to a measurable graph
topics.text: Substituting stress and strain into the modulus relation gives extension proportional to added force. Put force F on the horizontal axis and extension δ on the vertical axis. The gradient s then has units metres per newton and equals L divided by AY. Calculate modulus using the inverse of this gradient. Reversing the graph axes reverses the gradient, so always label axes before choosing a formula.
topics.question: What does a steeper extension–force line mean for equal wire dimensions?
topics.answer: It means more extension per newton and therefore a smaller Young modulus.

topics.title: Diameter measurement and sensitivity
topics.text: The micrometer reading must be corrected for any verified zero error. Take readings at several positions and rotate the instrument around the wire to detect nonuniformity or an oval cross section. Use gentle, repeatable contact rather than squeezing the wire. Diameter enters the area as a square; consequently a small fractional diameter error has approximately twice that fractional effect on area and inferred modulus. Repeated measurements reveal variation but cannot remove a shared calibration error.
topics.question: If diameter is overestimated, how is the calculated modulus affected?
topics.answer: The calculated area is too large, so the inferred modulus is too small for the same measured gradient.

topics.title: Reference readings, settling and unloading
topics.text: A small initial tension can straighten a real wire. Define zero extension after this setup condition and express subsequent forces as additional forces relative to it. Wait for movement to settle before reading. An unloaded repeat checks whether the apparatus slips or the specimen retains deformation. A constant indicator offset can appear as a graph intercept; it should be investigated rather than automatically forcing a fit through zero.
topics.question: Why subtract an initial indicator reading?
topics.answer: The difference isolates the extension caused by the added force and removes a constant reading offset.
topics.formula: δ = reading with added force − reference reading

topics.title: Units, fit quality and uncertainty
topics.text: For this specimen the predicted gradient is about 0.05093 mm/N, corresponding to 0.1019 mm extension at 2 N and 1.0186 mm at 20 N. Convert a graph gradient expressed in mm/N to m/N before calculating pascals. Examine deviations from the fitted line, not only the final modulus. Scatter in a fitted gradient captures only one part of uncertainty; length, diameter, force calibration, indicator resolution and temperature can also contribute. An ideal data set may have zero scatter while real measurement uncertainty remains finite.
topics.question: How do you convert 0.05093 mm/N to SI units?
topics.answer: Multiply by 0.001 to obtain 0.00005093 m/N.

procedure.title: Inspect and define the specimen
procedure.text: Check the clamp, identify the fixed gauge endpoints, and record the 2.000 m gauge length. Note that the animation exaggerates extension.
procedure.why: The length in the calculation must correspond to the length whose extension is measured.

procedure.title: Measure the diameter
procedure.text: Check micrometer zero, measure at several positions in two orientations, and record a representative mean diameter. Use 0.500 mm for the virtual specimen.
procedure.why: The circular cross-sectional area is calculated from diameter squared.

procedure.title: Set the reference
procedure.text: Straighten the wire with the setup tension and establish the extension reference. Treat displayed force as added force relative to that reference.
procedure.why: Slack removal and a defined baseline prevent apparent extension from being confused with tensile deformation.

procedure.title: Increase force in steps
procedure.text: Select an added force of 2 N, allow settling, and record extension. Repeat at 4, 6, 8 and 10 N or continue through the allowed 20 N range.
procedure.why: Several well-separated readings reveal the proportional relation and support a gradient estimate.

procedure.title: Check repeatability
procedure.text: Revisit one load and then remove the added load. In a real lab, record unloading readings and inspect for slip, drift or residual extension.
procedure.why: Agreement checks whether the chosen linear model remains appropriate and the reference is stable.

procedure.title: Fit and calculate
procedure.text: Plot extension against added force, obtain the gradient, convert it to m/N, calculate A = πd²/4 and then Y = L/(As). Report Y in GPa with the model assumptions.
procedure.why: A fitted gradient uses the whole set of observations and keeps the connection between the graph and the material property explicit.

precautions: In a physical lab secure clamps and keep feet clear of suspended loads; use a load catcher and follow the apparatus load limit.
Add loads gently, keep the wire straight, and wait until oscillation stops before taking a reading.
Use consistent micrometer contact and check for zero error, diameter variation and parallax where applicable.
Avoid temperature drift and do not extend a real specimen beyond the established proportional range.

quiz.question: Your graph plots extension vertically and force horizontally. Which expression gives modulus?
quiz.explanation: For δ = FL/(AY), the extension–force gradient is L/(AY), so Y = L/(As).

quiz.question: A wire of the same material and diameter has twice the gauge length. What happens to extension at the same force?
quiz.explanation: Extension is proportional to gauge length when force, area and modulus are unchanged.

quiz.question: Why is a perfect straight line insufficient to prove zero uncertainty?
options: A straight line always indicates plastic deformation
Geometry and calibration can still be uncertain
quiz.explanation: Common errors in diameter, length or force can shift the inferred modulus without creating visible scatter.

limitations: This is an ideal, uniform circular wire with constant modulus and small deformation. Added force is measured from a reference state; wire weight, support motion, creep, temperature change, calibration errors and plasticity are not modeled. The extension drawing is exaggerated for visibility. Perfect simulated readings demonstrate the equation and do not establish the uncertainty achievable with physical equipment. Fit scatter alone is not a complete uncertainty budget.

title: Viscosity by Stokes’ falling-sphere method
settings: Sphere density ρₛ = 2500 kg m⁻³; liquid density ρₗ = 1260 kg m⁻³.
Gate separation s = 0.100 m; gravity g = 9.80665 m s⁻².
Timing starts after terminal speed is reached and is rounded to 0.01 s.
modelExtra: The Newtonian liquid has a model viscosity of 1.20 Pa s at a fixed temperature. An effectively unbounded liquid is assumed. The simulated Reynolds number stays below 0.004 across the allowed radii. There are no wall/end corrections or temperature changes. Pre-terminal motion is not timed; the displayed fall is accelerated and not to scale.
aim: Determine the dynamic viscosity of a liquid from the terminal speeds of small spheres and the gradient of a speed–radius-squared graph.
intro: A small sphere sinking through a thick liquid reaches a steady speed when gravity is balanced by buoyancy and viscous drag. Time several sphere sizes across the same marked distance, convert times to speeds, and investigate the predicted square dependence on radius. The virtual fluid has density 1260 kg/m³ and model viscosity 1.200 Pa·s; sphere density is 2500 kg/m³. Radii range from 0.300 to 0.900 mm.

apparatus.name: Liquid column with two timing marks
apparatus.purpose: Provide a 0.100 m timing distance below the initial settling region.

apparatus.name: Spherical beads
apparatus.purpose: Provide smooth spheres of known density and different measured radii.

apparatus.name: Micrometer and ruler
apparatus.purpose: Measure sphere diameter and vertical separation of the timing marks.

apparatus.name: Timer and thermometer
apparatus.purpose: Record transit time and monitor liquid temperature, which affects viscosity.

topics.title: Dynamic viscosity: resistance to shear
topics.text: A Newtonian liquid supports a shear stress proportional to the rate at which adjacent layers slide past one another. Dynamic viscosity η is the proportionality factor, measured in pascal seconds. It is distinct from density: liquids of similar density can have very different flow resistance. In this model the liquid is uniform, Newtonian and maintained at fixed temperature, so one constant viscosity describes every run.
topics.question: Is viscosity the same physical quantity as density?
topics.answer: No. Density measures mass per volume; dynamic viscosity measures resistance to shearing motion.

topics.title: Three forces on a falling sphere
topics.text: Gravity acts downward with the weight of the sphere. The surrounding liquid exerts an upward buoyancy equal to the weight of displaced liquid. Once the sphere moves downward, drag also acts upward. Subtracting buoyancy from weight gives the driving force associated with the difference in densities. A sphere denser than the liquid sinks; this lesson uses a positive density difference of 1240 kg/m³.
topics.question: Why is sphere density alone insufficient in the calculation?
topics.answer: The liquid supports part of the sphere's weight through buoyancy, so the relevant driving force depends on the density difference.

topics.title: Stokes drag and creeping flow
topics.text: For a smooth sphere moving slowly through a Newtonian liquid far from boundaries, Stokes drag is proportional to viscosity, sphere radius and speed. This relation assumes creeping flow, where fluid inertia is negligible compared with viscous effects. A smooth-looking fall alone is not a sufficient test: the Reynolds number must also be small. The virtual parameters keep it below 0.01 over the complete radius range.
topics.question: What happens to Stokes drag if speed doubles at fixed radius and viscosity?
topics.answer: It doubles because Stokes drag is directly proportional to speed.

topics.title: Terminal velocity is a balance of forces
topics.text: At release the sphere can accelerate. As its speed rises, the drag increases until the downward effective weight and upward drag balance. At terminal velocity its acceleration is zero while it continues moving. Equating the two forces produces a speed proportional to r² and inversely proportional to η. Timing begins only after the settling region, so the calculation uses a steady transit speed rather than an average over initial acceleration.
topics.question: Does zero acceleration at terminal velocity mean that the sphere has stopped?
topics.answer: No. Its speed is constant and nonzero because the forces balance.

topics.title: Timing a known distance
topics.text: Use the centre of the sphere to identify both mark crossings consistently. Divide the fixed mark separation by elapsed physical time. Repeat timing for each size when using real equipment to assess scatter. The animation runs faster than real transit time; its displayed timer represents the modeled physical time, not wall-clock viewing time. For the 0.100 m gate, the model takes about 493 s at radius 0.300 mm and 54.8 s at 0.900 mm.
topics.question: If you accidentally time part of the acceleration region, how can viscosity be biased?
topics.answer: The average measured speed can be too low, leading to an overestimated viscosity when the terminal-speed formula is used.

topics.title: The straight-line graph and its gradient
topics.text: Place r² in square metres on the horizontal axis and terminal speed in metres per second on the vertical axis. The gradient s has units inverse metre per second and is 2Δρg/(9η). A larger gradient means larger speeds for the same radius and hence a smaller inferred viscosity. Convert radius from millimetres to metres before squaring; squaring a millimetre value first requires a factor of one million when converting to square metres.
topics.question: If radius doubles while other parameters stay fixed, how does terminal speed change?
topics.answer: It becomes four times as large because speed is proportional to radius squared.

topics.title: Checking the model and reporting uncertainty
topics.text: Calculate a Reynolds number for each recorded speed using sphere diameter as the length scale. At the largest permitted radius the predicted value is about 0.00345, comfortably below 0.01. In a real narrow tube, nearby walls increase drag and can make an uncorrected viscosity appear too high. Temperature drift, bead size, density and timing also matter. Regression uncertainty describes scatter about the chosen line; it does not include all these systematic contributions.
topics.question: Does a small Reynolds number eliminate the need to consider tube walls?
topics.answer: No. Creeping flow can still be strongly influenced by nearby walls; the unbounded-fluid assumption must be checked separately.

procedure.title: Record the controlled conditions
procedure.text: Record sphere density 2500 kg/m³, liquid density 1260 kg/m³ and g = 9.80665 m/s². In a physical lab also record temperature and confirm the liquid is suitable for a falling-sphere method.
procedure.why: Density difference, gravity and temperature enter the interpretation of terminal speed.

procedure.title: Measure sphere sizes
procedure.text: Measure each sphere diameter in several orientations, halve it to obtain radius, and convert to metres before calculating r². Select virtual radii within 0.300–0.900 mm.
procedure.why: The result depends on radius squared, making size measurement especially influential.

procedure.title: Define the timing gate
procedure.text: Set the vertical mark separation to 0.100 m below the release region. Release the sphere gently away from walls and verify steady motion before the upper mark.
procedure.why: The terminal-speed equation does not apply to timing that includes initial acceleration.

procedure.title: Time and record each transit
procedure.text: Time the sphere centre between the marks and record radius, r², distance and physical elapsed time. Repeat for several radii; the animation accelerates viewing while retaining modeled physical time.
procedure.why: Consistent crossing definitions and multiple sizes produce comparable observations.

procedure.title: Convert times to speeds
procedure.text: For each row calculate v = H/t. Fit v against r² and inspect the points and intercept. Calculate a trial viscosity and Reynolds number to check the creeping-flow condition.
procedure.why: A model should be checked against its assumptions before interpreting a fitted parameter.

procedure.title: Determine viscosity and assess limits
procedure.text: Use the gradient in η = 2(ρs − ρl)g/(9s). State viscosity in Pa·s, report the low Reynolds numbers and discuss temperature, walls, radius and timing as uncertainty sources.
procedure.why: A numerical answer is meaningful only together with the conditions under which it was inferred.

precautions: Use a clean, smooth sphere, avoid trapped bubbles, and release gently near the column centre.
Begin timing below the initial settling region and use the same sphere-centre crossing rule at both marks.
Maintain and record liquid temperature; allow disturbances from a previous fall to settle before repeating.
In a real setup assess wall and end effects, check sphere size and density, and verify low Reynolds number before using the unbounded Stokes formula.

quiz.question: Which two upward forces oppose a sinking sphere?
quiz.explanation: Weight acts downward. Buoyancy and drag oppose the downward motion.

quiz.question: Which graph is linear for the stated Stokes model?
quiz.explanation: The force balance gives vt = 2Δρgr²/(9η), so vt is proportional to r².

quiz.question: An unnoticed wall effect slows the sphere. Using the uncorrected formula will tend to give what result?
quiz.explanation: Viscosity inferred from a fixed radius is inversely proportional to speed, so an artificially low speed increases the result.

limitations: The calculation assumes an isolated rigid sphere in an unbounded, incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant density and viscosity and creeping flow. The illustrated column is a schematic timing gate; its walls exert no modeled correction. Initial acceleration, wall and end effects, bubbles, nonspherical beads and temperature drift are omitted. Timing starts after terminal motion is established. Virtual animation time is accelerated; reported elapsed time is physical model time. A fit error or perfect simulated line is not a complete experimental uncertainty estimate.

title: Focal length of a convex lens by the u–v method
settings: Thin converging lens; all object distances exceed its focal length.
u and v are positive real-object and real-image distance magnitudes.
Distances are measured from the lens principal plane; screen scale spacing 0.1 cm.
modelExtra: The lens has a model focal length of 15.0 cm and is treated as thin and paraxial. The scene is a schematic ray diagram. A screen setting within 0.05 cm of the ideal image plane is accepted; this tolerance represents half a 0.1 cm scale step, not optical depth of focus. Spherical/chromatic aberrations, lens thickness and alignment errors are omitted.
aim: Determine the focal length of one thin convex lens using focused object–image pairs, and test the thin-lens relationship with a reciprocal-distance graph.
intro: An image becoming larger does not mean that a lens has changed its focal length. In this experiment, keep one lens and move an illuminated object and a screen. Find several sharp images, measure both distances, and ask whether one focal length explains them all. The simulation uses a 15 cm ideal lens; the measurement task is to recover that value from observations.

apparatus.name: Illuminated arrow object
apparatus.purpose: Provides a recognisable shape so image orientation and sharpness can be judged.

apparatus.name: Thin convex lens and holder
apparatus.purpose: Refracts light into a real image when the object is beyond the focal point. Keep the same lens throughout the series.

apparatus.name: Movable screen
apparatus.purpose: Intercepts the image. Its location is adjusted manually until focus is achieved.

apparatus.name: Optical bench and distance scale
apparatus.purpose: Keeps object, lens and screen aligned and provides object and image distances from the lens plane.

topics.title: What focal length describes
topics.text: A converging lens directs paraxial rays parallel to its axis towards a focus. Focal length is the separation between the lens principal plane and that focus. For the ideal thin lens, the principal planes coincide with the drawn lens plane. Moving the object changes image location, while this lens property stays fixed.
topics.question: Does refocusing a screen change the lens focal length?
topics.answer: No. Refocusing locates a new image position for a different object distance.
topics.formula: f = distance from lens principal plane to principal focus

topics.title: Distances and the convention used here
topics.text: For this real-image measurement, u and v are positive distance magnitudes: u runs from the object to the lens plane, and v from the lens plane to the focused screen. Read them from the lens plane rather than from its holder edge. This convention differs from a Cartesian coordinate convention that assigns a negative coordinate to the object side.
topics.question: If the lens coordinate is 40 cm and the object coordinate is 10 cm, what is u?
topics.answer: u = 30 cm. It is the positive separation, not the object's coordinate.

topics.title: Connecting object and image positions
topics.text: The thin-lens equation relates the two measured separations to f. Rearranging it gives a direct focal-length estimate for each focused pair. Use one distance unit consistently. For u = 30.0 cm and v = 30.0 cm, the calculated focal length is 15.0 cm, rather than 30.0 cm.
topics.question: Why must an unfocused screen distance not be substituted as v?
topics.answer: v identifies the image plane. An arbitrary screen position does not satisfy the image-formation condition.

topics.title: Real images, virtual images and the focal boundary
topics.text: With u greater than f, rays meet beyond the lens and the image can be caught on a screen. At u = f, outgoing rays are parallel and there is no finite screen position for sharp focus. With 0 < u < f, a converging lens gives an upright virtual image on the object side; the screen method used here cannot measure it. Measurement controls therefore keep u between 22 and 70 cm.
topics.question: Can moving the screen farther away produce a sharp image when u = f?
topics.answer: No finite screen distance works in the ideal model.
topics.formula: v = fu/(u − f), for u > f

topics.title: Image size and ray construction
topics.text: A ray parallel to the axis refracts towards the far focus; a ray through the ideal thin-lens centre continues without deviation. Their intersection locates the image tip. Magnification is negative for this inverted real image. At u = 2f, v = 2f and image and object have equal size. Between f and 2f the real image is larger; beyond 2f it is smaller.
topics.question: What does m = −0.5 tell you?
topics.answer: The image is inverted and its height magnitude is half the object's height.

topics.title: A graph that tests the whole series
topics.text: Set x = 1/u and y = 1/v. The lens equation becomes y = −x + 1/f. Plot measured reciprocal distances, fit a line with a free slope, and compare it with the predicted slope of −1. The vertical intercept b has units cm⁻¹ when distances are in cm; its reciprocal gives f in cm. Do not force the slope to −1 and then describe the fitted slope as experimental confirmation.
topics.question: What focal length corresponds to b = 0.0667 cm⁻¹?

topics.title: Resolution, repeatability and systematic error
topics.text: Record focused distances to 0.1 cm. Rounding is not a complete uncertainty budget: real focus judgement, scale calibration and lens-plane offsets also matter. A shared wrong lens reference can bias every pair, even if their calculated focal lengths agree closely. Repeating a measurement tests repeatability, while checking the distance origin investigates a different possible error.
topics.question: Does a small spread of f values prove there is no systematic error?
topics.answer: No. A consistent reference-plane error can shift an entire set of otherwise repeatable measurements.
topics.formula: σ_f ≈ sqrt[(v² σ_u/(u+v)²)² + (u² σ_v/(u+v)²)²], for independent standard uncertainties

procedure.title: Align the bench
procedure.text: Place the illuminated object, lens centre and screen centre on a common axis. Establish the lens plane as the distance origin. In a physical lab, use a low-power lamp and keep the screen perpendicular to the bench.
procedure.why: Misalignment can hide the image or make its sharpest part difficult to judge.

procedure.title: Choose the first object position
procedure.text: Keep the same lens and set u = 25.0 cm. Predict the approximate image position before moving the screen. All suggested object positions exceed the 15 cm model focal length.
procedure.why: Selecting u > f ensures a real image is available for the screen method.

procedure.title: Find focus manually
procedure.text: Move the screen through the blurred image and bracket the sharpest position from both sides. The virtual bench accepts a reading only when the screen is within 0.05 cm of the ideal image plane; that tolerance is a software rule, not a claim about real visual precision.
procedure.why: A lens calculation requires the actual image-plane separation, rather than any screen coordinate.

procedure.title: Record one observation
procedure.text: Record u and the focused screen distance v to 0.1 cm. Note the inverted image and its relative size. Preserve the measured numbers before calculating f.
procedure.why: Separating observation from calculation prevents replacing measurements with desired theoretical values.

procedure.title: Repeat for a range of positions
procedure.text: Use u = 30.0, 35.0, 45.0 and 60.0 cm. Refocus for every new object position; do not leave the previous screen distance unchanged. Keep lens selection and distance units consistent.
procedure.why: Several pairs test whether one focal length explains different image positions.

procedure.title: Calculate and interpret
procedure.text: For each pair compute f = uv/(u+v), then plot 1/v against 1/u with labelled reciprocal units. Report the fitted slope, intercept, reciprocal-intercept focal length and limitations. Distinguish rounding differences from actual evidence of experimental noise.
procedure.why: The table and graph offer complementary checks of the model rather than a single convenient reading.

precautions: In a physical lab, use a lamp or LED object. Never view the Sun through the lens or use sunlight as the focusing source.
Measure from the lens principal-plane approximation and document holder offsets; read bench scales without parallax.
Keep the same lens for every row, align component heights, and judge focus using the same image feature.
Record observations before rounding calculations. A screen-focus acceptance indicator is a simulation aid unavailable on an ordinary optical bench.

quiz.question: For f = 15 cm and u = 30 cm, where is the real image?
Which graph should have slope −1 for one ideal thin lens?
quiz.explanation: Rearranging gives 1/v = −1/u + 1/f. Both axes must use reciprocal distances in the same units.

quiz.question: An object is placed 10 cm from a 15 cm converging lens. What should happen in this screen experiment?
options: A sharp image can be found by moving the screen
No real image can be focused onto the screen
quiz.explanation: The object is inside the focal length. The image is virtual, so it cannot be intercepted by this screen.

limitations: The simulation uses a monochromatic paraxial thin-lens model with a fixed 15 cm focal length. The ray diagram illustrates geometrical construction; it does not calculate diffraction, lens thickness, spherical or chromatic aberration, detector response, scattered light or actual image contrast. Focus is tested against a calculated plane with a 0.05 cm software tolerance and observations are displayed to 0.1 cm. These choices teach the measurement workflow but cannot establish real apparatus accuracy. For a real lens, identify its principal-plane approximation, assess focus range and scale uncertainty, and check alignment before interpreting agreement with the model.

title: Ohm’s law and resistance from a current–voltage graph
settings: Fixed ideal resistance: 100 Ω at constant temperature.
Voltage is across the resistor; current is in series, rounded to 0.01 mA.
Ideal supply and meters; maximum model power at 10 V is 1 W.
fitEquation: I = mV + b; R = 1/m (I in amperes)
aim: Determine the resistance of an ohmic conductor from the gradient of current against potential difference.
intro: Build the link between a circuit diagram, meter readings and a straight-line graph. Set a voltage across a resistor, measure its current and use several observations to estimate resistance. The readings here are generated by a fixed-temperature resistor model and are simulated data.

apparatus.name: Variable DC supply
apparatus.purpose: Apply 1–10 V across the resistor with the circuit switched off while wiring.

apparatus.name: 100 Ω model resistor
apparatus.purpose: Provide a constant resistance for the simulated comparison. A physical resistor must have an appropriate power rating.

apparatus.name: Ammeter and voltmeter
apparatus.purpose: Place the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.

apparatus.name: Switch and leads
apparatus.purpose: Complete secure connections and limit unnecessary heating between readings.

topics.title: Potential difference, current and resistance
topics.text: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge between two points. Current is charge passing a cross-section per unit time. Resistance compares the voltage across an element with the current through it. The ratio V/I can be defined at an operating point even for a nonlinear element; constant resistance over the tested range is the additional ohmic property.
topics.question: Is any device with a value of V/I necessarily ohmic?
topics.answer: No. An ohmic device has a constant ratio under fixed physical conditions over the range examined.
topics.formula: V = W/Q; I = dQ/dt; R = V/I

topics.title: The condition behind Ohm’s law
topics.text: For the model resistor the voltage and current are proportional while temperature and physical structure remain fixed. Raising voltage can heat a real resistor and change its resistance. A curved graph can reflect heating, a nonlinear element or measurement loading; inspect the circuit before treating it as a failure of the algebra.
topics.question: Why keep the resistor temperature stable?
topics.answer: Resistance can depend on temperature, so heating changes the system being tested.
topics.formula: V = IR at fixed physical conditions

topics.title: Correct meter connections
topics.text: A series ammeter measures the current through the resistor and should have low internal resistance. A parallel voltmeter measures the potential difference across the resistor and should have high input resistance. A real voltmeter also draws current: depending on the exact ammeter position, the ammeter can include that extra current or the voltmeter can include the ammeter voltage drop. Record the actual circuit topology.
topics.question: Why must an ammeter never be connected directly across the supply?
topics.answer: Its small resistance can draw a very large current, damaging the instrument or triggering its protection.
topics.formula: Ideal ammeter resistance → 0; ideal voltmeter resistance → ∞

topics.title: Read milliampere values in amperes
topics.text: The displayed current is in mA, but the numerical fit uses amperes. Divide a displayed mA value by 1000 before using SI equations. For example, 50.00 mA is 0.05000 A. The simulation rounds the current display to 0.01 mA. Resolution is a display increment, not an uncertainty budget or a manufacturer accuracy specification.
topics.question: What current in amperes corresponds to 25.00 mA?

topics.title: Choose and interpret the gradient
topics.text: Put voltage V on the horizontal axis and current I in amperes on the vertical axis. Fit I = mV + b, retaining the intercept. The gradient is conductance, measured in A/V or siemens. Therefore resistance is the reciprocal of the gradient. A graph with the axes exchanged instead has resistance as its gradient; always state which graph you used.
topics.question: For an I-versus-V graph, is the gradient R?
topics.answer: No. It is 1/R; R is the reciprocal of the gradient.

topics.title: Power, measurement limits and uncertainty
topics.text: Power dissipated in a resistor grows quadratically with voltage. At 10 V across 100 Ω the ideal current is 0.100 A and power is 1.0 W. That exceeds the continuous rating of common 0.25 W resistors; a physical apparatus needs an adequately rated component, current limiting and a suitable thermal procedure. For a fit-derived resistance, the gradient contribution is u(R) = u(m)/m². Meter calibration, voltage uncertainty, lead resistance and heating are additional effects, even if the virtual fit has zero residual.
topics.question: Can exact model points establish zero physical measurement uncertainty?
topics.answer: No. Exact agreement follows from the generator; a real uncertainty budget still includes instruments and operating conditions.

procedure.title: Identify the circuit
procedure.text: With the supply off, connect the resistor and ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the resistor. Check polarity and meter ranges.
procedure.why: Correct topology ensures the two meters describe the same element.

procedure.title: Choose a safe operating range
procedure.text: Begin at low voltage. For real apparatus check power rating and current limit before using the full range; keep temperature stable.
procedure.why: Heating can alter resistance and excessive power can damage a resistor.

procedure.title: Measure a voltage-current pair
procedure.text: Set the voltage and obtain the current. Record voltage in V and the displayed current in mA, including the display resolution.
procedure.why: A pair must refer to the same steady operating condition.

procedure.title: Collect a spread of observations
procedure.text: Take at least five voltage settings across the permitted range. Repeat if possible and compare increasing and decreasing voltage runs in a physical experiment.
procedure.why: A broad spread constrains the gradient; repeated or reversed runs can reveal drift.

procedure.title: Convert and fit
procedure.text: Convert mA to A and fit I = mV + b without forcing the intercept to zero. Inspect residuals and intercept.
procedure.why: The inverse-gradient formula requires amperes, and an intercept can expose offsets.

procedure.title: Report resistance
procedure.text: Calculate R = 1/m in Ω. State fit-only error separately from meter, loading and temperature uncertainties, and label these observations simulated.
procedure.why: A numerical resistance needs units and a defensible account of its limitations.

precautions: Switch off before changing physical connections; use correct meter sockets and ranges.
Never connect an ammeter directly across the supply.
Check resistor power rating; the model’s upper setting dissipates 1 W.
Minimize contact resistance and heating; record simulated observations as simulated.

quiz.question: The slope of current in A against voltage in V is 0.010 A/V. What is R?
quiz.explanation: For these axes R = 1/m = 100 Ω.

quiz.question: Where is the voltmeter connected?
options: Directly in place of the resistor
quiz.explanation: A voltmeter compares the two terminal potentials.

quiz.question: Which change can produce a curved physical I–V graph?
quiz.explanation: A temperature change can make resistance vary during the measurements.

limitations: This model assumes a constant 100 Ω resistance, exact applied voltage, an ideal ammeter and voltmeter, and no heating or lead resistance. Current is rounded to 0.01 mA. The chosen voltage grid can give perfectly collinear readings; a zero fit-only standard error is not a claim of zero laboratory uncertainty.
modelExtra: The generator uses I = V/100 and displays current in mA. Graph fitting converts current back to A and estimates R = 1/gradient. The supplied 100 Ω value is a model reference, not an independently measured result.

title: Unknown resistance using a metre bridge
settings: Unknown R is in the left gap; l is measured from the left end.
Fixed unknown R = 5 Ω; wire length 100 cm and uniform resistance per length.
Jockey scale resolution: 0.1 cm. Ideal galvanometer at null.
aim: Determine an unknown resistance using balance lengths on a metre bridge and a straight-line graph.
intro: Explore a null measurement instead of reading current directly. Change a known resistance, locate the balance point on a uniform wire and infer an unknown resistance from a ratio of lengths. All generated balances are simulated and use a 100.0 cm ideal wire.

apparatus.name: Uniform metre bridge wire
apparatus.purpose: Provide a 100.0 cm wire whose resistance is proportional to length.

apparatus.name: Unknown resistor in the left gap
apparatus.purpose: Connect the resistor R to the same side as the zero end used to measure balance length.

apparatus.name: Resistance box in the right gap
apparatus.purpose: Set the known resistance S in ohms.

apparatus.name: DC cell, key, galvanometer and jockey
apparatus.purpose: Detect a null using brief light contact; a physical galvanometer may require protective resistance.

topics.title: Bridge geometry and symbols
topics.text: Place the unknown R in the left gap and known S in the right gap. The wire runs from A at 0 cm to B at 100 cm. A galvanometer joins the gap junction to a movable jockey J on the wire. Define l as AJ, measured from the unknown-resistor end. A formula remembered without this orientation can invert the resistance ratio.
topics.question: From which end is l measured in this lesson?
topics.answer: From the 0 cm end adjacent to the unknown resistance R.
topics.formula: Left wire length = l; right wire length = L − l; L = 100.0 cm

topics.title: Why a null gives a ratio
topics.text: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so its two terminals are at equal potential. The gap resistors form one potential divider and the two wire segments form another. Equating the fractional voltage drops gives R/S equal to the ratio of the two wire resistances. This equality uses the null condition, not the assumption that all currents in the circuit are equal.
topics.question: Does zero galvanometer current mean every part of the bridge carries zero current?
topics.answer: No. Current still flows through the two main branches; only the detector branch is at null.

topics.title: Uniform wire and length ratio
topics.text: For a wire of uniform resistivity and cross-sectional area, each segment resistance is proportional to length. The common factor cancels in the ratio, giving R/S = l/(L − l). Both lengths must use the same unit. If S = R, the model balance lies at the midpoint. Wire nonuniformity and resistance at the ends disturb this ideal relation.
topics.question: What balance length is expected when R = S?
topics.answer: 50.0 cm for a 100.0 cm ideal bridge.
topics.formula: R = S l/(100.0 − l), with l in cm

topics.title: From balance readings to a straight line
topics.text: Rearrange the bridge equation as (100.0 − l)/l = S/R. Plot known resistance S in Ω horizontally and the dimensionless ratio y = (100.0 − l)/l vertically. The slope has unit Ω⁻¹ and equals 1/R; R = 1/m. A free intercept helps reveal systematic departures but cannot correct every end effect.
topics.question: What is the vertical-axis unit?
topics.answer: It is dimensionless because it is a ratio of two lengths in the same unit.

topics.title: Why central balances are preferred
topics.text: For a fixed absolute length uncertainty, the relative resistance error from l is approximately L u(l)/[l(L − l)]. This is smallest near the midpoint and grows towards either end. Choose S similar to R in a physical experiment so balances usually lie near the centre; an exploratory range can demonstrate why end positions are less suitable. The available 1 Ω setting gives a balance near 83.3 cm and should not be treated as a preferred physical setting.
topics.question: Does a balance very close to an end improve precision?
topics.answer: No. The ratio becomes highly sensitive to a small length error.
topics.formula: u(R)/R ≈ L u(l)/[l(L − l)] for the length contribution

topics.title: Reversal, contact effects and uncertainty
topics.text: In physical work exchange R and S, measure the new balance from the same geometric zero, and apply the corresponding reversed formula R = S(L − l_reversed)/l_reversed. Compare both determinations; interchange can diagnose and reduce some end effects, without removing arbitrary wire nonuniformity. Include uncertainty of S, null detection and l, and inspect drift. Ordinary least squares here treats S as exact and does not weight the transformed length uncertainties.
topics.question: After interchanging the gap resistors, can the original formula be used unchanged?
topics.answer: No. The orientation has changed, so the resistance ratio must be written for the new arrangement.

procedure.title: Fix the orientation
procedure.text: Connect unknown R in the left gap and known S in the right gap. Mark the wire zero at the unknown side and use L = 100.0 cm.
procedure.why: The resistance-length equation depends on the side assignment.

procedure.title: Set a known resistance
procedure.text: Select S, starting near 5 Ω in this model to place the expected null near the midpoint.
procedure.why: Central balance points are less sensitive to length reading error.

procedure.title: Find the null
procedure.text: Close the cell key and touch the jockey lightly at trial positions until galvanometer deflection passes through zero. In this simulation request the model balance reading.
procedure.why: A null compares potentials without drawing detector current at balance.

procedure.title: Record and repeat
procedure.text: Record S and l to the shown resolution. Collect at least five distinct S values, preferably keeping physical balances around the central portion.
procedure.why: Several balances support a graph and allow comparison of separate R estimates.

procedure.title: Calculate graph variables
procedure.text: For each reading calculate L − l and y = (L − l)/l. Fit y against S with a free intercept.
procedure.why: This transformation makes the reciprocal unknown resistance the gradient.

procedure.title: Interpret the result
procedure.text: Calculate R = 1/m in Ω and compare individual values S l/(L − l). In real apparatus interchange the gap resistors and use the reversed formula, then discuss end effects and uncertainties.
procedure.why: Consistency across settings and orientations provides a stronger check than one balance.

precautions: Define l from the unknown-resistance end and keep both lengths in the same unit.
Touch the jockey gently and briefly; do not drag it along a live wire.
Use small currents and open the key between physical readings to limit heating.
Prefer balances near the middle, check resistance-box contacts and distinguish model readings from real observations.

quiz.question: With unknown R in the left gap and known S in the right, which formula is correct?
quiz.explanation: The left-gap ratio matches the left-wire ratio.

quiz.question: At balance the galvanometer current is zero. What follows?
options: The detector terminals are at equal potential
Both gap resistors must equal zero
quiz.explanation: A null is equality of the detector terminal potentials.

quiz.question: Why choose a balance near 50 cm?
options: A fixed length error has a smaller relative effect
The wire no longer needs to be uniform
quiz.explanation: The factor L/[l(L − l)] is smallest at the midpoint.

limitations: The simulated wire is exactly uniform and 100.0 cm long. End resistances, jockey resistance, heating, thermoelectric offsets and galvanometer sensitivity are omitted. The unknown resistor is fixed at 5 Ω and known resistance settings are exact. Balance lengths are rounded to 0.1 cm; resulting fit scatter reflects quantization rather than a complete measurement uncertainty.
modelExtra: The model places unknown R = 5 Ω on the left and known S on the right. It computes l = 100R/(R + S), rounded to 0.1 cm. The fitted graph uses x = S and y = (100 − l)/l, so resistance is 1/gradient. Range endpoints are available for sensitivity exploration; real measurements should favor central balances.

title: RC charging and the capacitor time constant
settings: Supply E = 5.000 V; resistance R = 10.00 kΩ.
Capacitance C = 100.0 μF; model time constant τ = RC = 1.000 s.
Initially uncharged ideal capacitor; voltage rounded to 0.001 V.
fitEquation: Vc = E(1 − exp(−t/τ)); ln[E/(E − Vc)] = mt + b; τ = 1/m
aim: Determine the charging time constant of an RC circuit from capacitor-voltage observations and a logarithmic graph.
intro: Watch a capacitor approach its final voltage and turn an exponential curve into a straight line. Record capacitor voltage at several elapsed times, transform the readings and estimate the time constant. Every virtual observation starts from an initially discharged capacitor; these are simulated transients.

apparatus.name: 5.000 V DC step source
apparatus.purpose: Provide a constant applied voltage E from t = 0.

apparatus.name: 10.0 kΩ resistor
apparatus.purpose: Limit charging current and set the resistance in the model time constant.

apparatus.name: 100 μF capacitor
apparatus.purpose: Store charge; preserve polarity and voltage rating when using a physical polarized capacitor.

apparatus.name: Switch and voltage-time recorder
apparatus.purpose: Start charging from an initially discharged state and sample capacitor voltage with adequate time resolution.

topics.title: Charge storage and voltage
topics.text: A capacitor stores equal and opposite charge on its conductors. For a linear capacitor, stored charge is proportional to its terminal voltage. Initially discharged means Vc(0) = 0. With finite series resistance the capacitor voltage changes continuously; current initially has its largest value and then decreases.
topics.question: Can the capacitor voltage jump instantly in this finite-current model?
topics.answer: No. An instantaneous voltage step would require an impulse of charging current.
topics.formula: Q = C Vc; I = dQ/dt = C dVc/dt

topics.title: Derive the charging equation
topics.text: Kirchhoff’s loop rule gives E = IR + Vc. Substitute I = C dVc/dt and solve the first-order differential equation with Vc(0) = 0. The voltage difference E − Vc decays exponentially even though Vc itself grows. These equations require a constant source, constant R and C, and negligible leakage and instrument loading.
topics.question: Which quantity decays exponentially during charging?
topics.answer: The remaining difference E − Vc, and also the charging current.
topics.formula: RC dVc/dt + Vc = E; Vc(t) = E[1 − exp(−t/RC)]

topics.title: What one time constant means
topics.text: Define τ = RC. After one τ the voltage has reached 1 − 1/e, about 63.2%, of E and current has dropped to 1/e of its initial value. After three τ the voltage is about 95.0% of E. It approaches E asymptotically; no finite ideal time makes it exactly equal to E. For 10,000 Ω and 100 × 10⁻⁶ F, τ is 1.000 s.
topics.question: Is τ the time to reach 100% of the final voltage?
topics.answer: No. It is the time to reach about 63.2% from an initially discharged state.

topics.title: Make the logarithm dimensionless
topics.text: Rearrange E − Vc = E exp(−t/τ). Taking a natural logarithm of E/(E − Vc) gives a positive transformed variable y = t/τ. This ratio is dimensionless. Do not use log base ten without its conversion factor and do not take the logarithm of an unnormalized voltage value. Valid charging readings satisfy 0 ≤ Vc < E.
topics.question: What happens to ln[E/(E − Vc)] at Vc = E?
topics.answer: It is undefined because the denominator is zero; such a reading cannot be transformed.

topics.title: Fit the correct sign and gradient
topics.text: Plot time t in seconds on the horizontal axis and y = ln[E/(E − Vc)] vertically. Fit y = mt + b. The gradient is positive, has units s⁻¹, and τ = 1/m. If instead plotting ln[(E − Vc)/E], the slope would be negative and τ = −1/m. Retain an intercept: a timing offset or incomplete initial discharge can shift it.
topics.question: For the positive logarithm used here, what does a gradient 2 s⁻¹ imply?
topics.formula: m = 1/τ; τ = 1/m; C = τ/R if R is independently known

topics.title: Sampling, transformation and uncertainty
topics.text: With τ near one second, manual stopwatch-and-meter readings may be too slow; use synchronized data acquisition or an oscilloscope with adequate sampling. Rounding voltage to 0.001 V becomes increasingly influential as Vc approaches E, because dy/dVc = 1/(E − Vc). Source uncertainty is also amplified near the asymptote. The transformed observations therefore need not have equal uncertainty; an unweighted fit is a teaching simplification. Fit-only u(τ) = u(m)/m² excludes resistor tolerance, capacitor tolerance, loading and clock calibration.
topics.question: Why avoid treating near-final transformed readings as equally precise?
topics.answer: A small voltage error is magnified when E − Vc is small.

procedure.title: Prepare the discharged state
procedure.text: With a physical source disconnected, discharge through a suitable resistor and verify near-zero capacitor voltage. Check component polarity and ratings before wiring.
procedure.why: The model solution requires Vc(0) = 0 and safe physical handling requires controlled discharge.

procedure.title: Set the source and timing reference
procedure.text: Use E = 5.000 V and identify t = 0 as the start of the applied voltage step. Choose a recording method suited to a roughly one-second transient.
procedure.why: A time-origin error changes the transformed intercept.

procedure.title: Read the charging voltage
procedure.text: Choose an elapsed time in the 0.2–3.0 s range and request the capacitor-voltage observation. Record Vc in volts and time in seconds.
procedure.why: The measured quantity is capacitor voltage, not resistor voltage.

procedure.title: Gather distinct times
procedure.text: Collect at least five distinct times across the range. Each model observation restarts the same initially discharged transient; real repeat runs require a verified discharge first.
procedure.why: A common initial condition makes measurements comparable.

procedure.title: Transform and plot
procedure.text: Check that Vc is below E. Calculate E − Vc, then the dimensionless ratio E/(E − Vc), then its natural logarithm. Fit this logarithm against time.
procedure.why: The positive logarithm yields a positive slope equal to 1/τ.

procedure.title: Calculate and assess
procedure.text: Use τ = 1/m in seconds. Compare with RC = 1.000 s, inspect the intercept and residuals, and discuss voltage-dependent transformed uncertainty and timing calibration.
procedure.why: Agreement with model components is a consistency check rather than independent proof of their accuracy.

precautions: Check capacitor polarity and voltage rating; discharge through an appropriate resistor before reconnecting physical components.
Measure actual source voltage in physical work and use the same E in every transformation.
Use natural logarithms of dimensionless ratios; exclude Vc ≥ E from this analysis.
Use synchronized fast recording and reset to a discharged state before each physical repeat; label virtual data simulated.

quiz.question: What fraction of E has an initially discharged capacitor reached at t = τ?
quiz.explanation: Charging gives Vc/E = 1 − exp(−1).

quiz.question: What is the slope of ln[E/(E − Vc)] against t?
quiz.explanation: The positive ratio gives y = t/τ.

quiz.question: Why do rounded voltages near E create large logarithmic errors?
options: Natural logarithms change to base ten
quiz.explanation: A small remaining voltage makes the transformation highly sensitive to voltage error.

limitations: The model uses E = 5.000 V, R = 10,000 Ω and C = 100 μF, with zero initial voltage, instantaneous source switching, exact elapsed times and no leakage, equivalent series resistance, dielectric absorption or meter loading. Vc is rounded to 0.001 V. Each requested observation starts an identical transient. The unweighted logarithmic fit treats times as exact and does not model the voltage-dependent uncertainty introduced by transformation.
modelExtra: The generator calculates Vc = 5[1 − exp(−t/1.000)] V and rounds to 0.001 V. Analysis uses x = t and y = ln[5/(5 − Vc)], estimating τ = 1/gradient. The reference 1.000 s is the product of the fixed model R and C, not a measurement of actual components.

title: Refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope
settings: Plane parallel ideal glass; air index taken as 1; fixed glass index n = 1.500.
Paraxial normal viewing; focus-based apparent depth rounded to 0.01 mm.
Aligned microscope datum: R₁ = 0; R₂ = real depth; R₃ = R₂ − apparent depth.
fitEquation: n = t/a; a = mt + b; n = 1/m
aim: Determine the refractive index of a plane-parallel glass slab from microscope measurements of real and apparent depth, then compare individual ratios with a straight-line estimate.
intro: A mark below glass appears closer to the upper surface than it really is. Use this apparent rise to connect refraction with a measurable depth. Vary slab thickness, collect simulated apparent-depth readings, and infer refractive index from their graph. The virtual apparatus uses one glass material and one fixed wavelength; changing thickness does not change its index.

apparatus.name: Travelling microscope
apparatus.purpose: Focus successively on a bare mark, its image through glass and a marker on the upper surface; read the same vertical carriage scale each time.

apparatus.name: Plane-parallel glass slabs
apparatus.purpose: Provide different real thicknesses of the same transparent material, with model refractive index 1.500 relative to air.

apparatus.name: Fine base mark and surface marker
apparatus.purpose: Identify the lower object and the upper surface without confusing their focus positions.

apparatus.name: Levelled support and scale
apparatus.purpose: Keep the viewing axis close to the surface normal and express all vertical differences in consistent units.

topics.title: Refraction and the raised image
topics.text: Rays travelling from glass into air bend away from the normal. An observer traces the emerging rays backwards and locates a virtual image above the actual mark. The mark itself has not moved. A microscope can focus on this image even though a screen placed at its apparent location would not collect a real image there.
topics.question: Does the glass physically lift the mark?
topics.answer: No. Refraction changes the apparent origin of the emerging rays; the object stays at the base.

topics.title: Deriving the depth ratio
topics.text: Let t be real depth below a flat surface and a be apparent depth measured from that same surface. For a narrow ray bundle near the normal, ray geometry and Snell's law give a approximately equal to t divided by the glass-to-air index. This approximation becomes less reliable for strongly oblique viewing. Both depths must share the same upper reference plane.
topics.question: Why must the microscope view nearly normally?
topics.answer: The simple depth ratio uses paraxial rays. At larger angles a single constant apparent depth is no longer an adequate description.

topics.title: Three focus positions, two depth differences
topics.text: Use an upward-increasing height scale. Define R1 as the focus height of the mark with no slab, R2 as the upper surface focus height and R3 as the apparent mark focus height through glass. Then real depth is R2 minus R1 and apparent depth is R2 minus R3. The apparent rise R3 minus R1 is a different quantity. Labels vary between apparatus instructions, so identify the physical focus positions before subtracting.
topics.question: If R1 = 0.00 mm, R2 = 9.00 mm and R3 = 3.00 mm, what is apparent depth?
topics.answer: It is 9.00 minus 3.00 = 6.00 mm. The 3.00 mm rise is not the apparent depth.
topics.formula: t = R2 − R1; a = R2 − R3; rise = t − a

topics.title: From depth readings to a fitted index
topics.text: Plot apparent depth a vertically against real depth t horizontally. A single material gives a straight line with slope s = 1/n; the fitted estimate is n = 1/s. Fit an intercept rather than forcing zero: a nonzero value can reveal a persistent focus or datum error. A ratio from one observation is a useful calculation check, but the graph combines the range of thicknesses.
topics.question: What does the slope mean when both axes use millimetres?
topics.answer: It is a dimensionless depth ratio, equal to 1/n. The slope is unchanged if both axes are converted to metres.

topics.title: Resolution and shared errors
topics.text: The simulator rounds apparent depth to 0.01 mm. That is display resolution, not a complete physical uncertainty. In a real measurement, focus judgement, backlash and scale calibration matter. Since R2 is used in both depth differences, their errors can be correlated. A basic least-squares fit treats real depth as exact; report this limitation rather than interpreting tiny residuals as proof of high precision.
topics.question: Are errors in real and apparent depth necessarily independent?
topics.answer: No. Both contain the same upper-surface reading, so its error influences both derived quantities.

topics.title: Material identity and model limits
topics.text: Refractive index depends on material and wavelength. Different thicknesses should therefore be specimens of the same glass under the same illumination. Combining unlike glasses does not test one common straight line. The reference 1.500 is a model choice, not a universal value for all glass. Air is treated as index one and the simulation ignores surface roughness, dispersion and optical aberrations.
topics.question: Can changing only thickness change the model index?
topics.answer: No. Thickness changes both depths proportionally; material and wavelength remain fixed.

procedure.title: Define the scale and focus references
procedure.text: Level the microscope and identify an upward-increasing vertical scale. Focus the crosshairs first, then focus the bare base mark and label its carriage height R1.
procedure.why: A clear reference and sharp crosshairs prevent sign mistakes and focus ambiguity.
